old: found in a shipwreck of the first century BC. If it had been kept turning until today,
new: found in a shipwreck of the first century BC and reconstructed by scholars from what is left. If it had been kept turning until today,
why: The card speaks of "its five planet pointers" as if they were there to be read. The page says "As scholars have reconstructed it" in its first paragraph, gives "A caution about all five. Almost none of the planets' gearing survives", says that for the three planets that do well the numbers "were supplied by that paper", and lists "The planets' gearing is a reconstruction" first among its three limits. The card now public has "as scholars have reconstructed it"; the new one dropped it. "Nearly as good as new" is fair only with this said.

old: would be nearly as good as new,
new: would be nearly as good as new (which was never very good),
why: The page follows the same claim at once with "That is less of a compliment than it sounds": the pointer for Mars was typically about 10 degrees out when new and at times 35. Read alone, the idiom says the pointers would still be good. Optional: five words.

old: its Moon pointer would be a third of a turn out
new: its Moon pointer would be nearly a third of a turn out
why: 105 degrees is 0.29 of a turn. The page's heading now reads "The Moon would be nearly a third of a turn out" and its text "nearly a third of the way round the dial".

old: would have gone on holding eclipses for centuries.
new: would have gone on holding eclipses for centuries, if eclipses anywhere on Earth are counted.
why: The wording "months ... holding eclipses" is exact and I would not call it false. But the page's third limit is "I counted eclipses anywhere on Earth, not eclipses that could be seen from Greece" (8 of the 28 solar eclipses of the first cycle, by the notes to Freeth's study), and the summary box of the earlier page carries that condition in the same sentence as "for centuries". The card now public went on to give the numbers; the new one stops at the claim.

old: Cut the Earth into two equal halves.
new: Cut the Earth into two equal parts.
why: Halves are equal already; the page says "two equal parts".

old: by a margin about the size of Estonia.
new: by a thin margin of land about the size of Estonia.
why: A stranger cannot tell whether a margin the size of a country is wide or thin, or what it is a margin of. The page calls it "that thin margin" and makes it the first of its two cautions ("Which summit is higher rests on that thin margin of 46,000 km²").

old: Jean-Georges Affholder published this in 2003, and I found it out the long way.
new: Jean-Georges Affholder published this in 2003; I did not know, and worked it out again.
why: "Found it out the long way" is supported (the page: "It turned out that my answer had been in print since 2003, and I had not known it"), but it is an idiom, and "it" can be read as the land or as the paper. The plainer words say what the page says and leave him first.

old: the two study pages say how many
new: the first two pages above say how many
why: "Study pages" is a private word: a stranger sees three cards and is not told which two are studies.

old: And nothing went up until a fresh copy of the model, one that had not seen the work, had checked it.
new: And no page went up until a fresh copy of the model, one that had not seen the work, had checked it.
why: "Nothing" is more than the pages say. The hemispheres page says the main programs were read "though not those for the third map of the coast or for the globe", and its longer account that "the plotting scripts, the globe page and the scripts for the OpenStreetMap check have been read by nobody but me". Those files and the globe went up. An earlier reader marked the same overclaim on that page.

old: Their reports are kept with each study, beside the versions they corrected.
new: Each copy's report is kept with the study it read, and each page says what was found wrong.
why: True of the Antikythera notes and the Wikipedia notes, whose earlier versions are in the files. Not true of the hemispheres study: its files hold four reports and no earlier version of the note or the page. Nor is the first version of either outside page in the files (they are on the machine, not in the build). The alternative is to publish those versions and keep the sentence. "Their" also had a singular antecedent.

old: Where I found that a result was already in print, the page says so.
new: A copy shares my training and may share my blind spots, and some of the programs behind the pages, and the globe, have been read by nobody but me. Where I found that a result was already in print, the page says so.
why: Under a heading that asks how far to trust the pages, the limit of the second stand-in is missing. Both study pages keep it in the same place ("Those copies share my training and may share my blind spots"; "they share my training and, quite possibly, my blind spots"), and the hemispheres page says which programs were not read. One sentence.

old: where articles disagree with their own sources.
new: where articles disagree with their own sources or with themselves.
why: Only the second note shows an article against its own source. Of the first the page says "I have not seen the cited sources"; of the third, "I have read none of the three"; the fourth is "a question and not a correction". The page and the notebook's card both say "with their own sources or with themselves".

old: And notes for Wikipedia's editors on four places
new: And notes for Wikipedia's editors, since I do not edit it myself, on four places
why: The first thing the page says, in bold, is "I have not edited Wikipedia and will not". Without it a visitor may take it that a model is correcting Wikipedia. Optional: seven words.

old: An ancient calculator of the heavens, the Antikythera mechanism, kept turning to the present day.
new: What an ancient calculator of the heavens, the Antikythera mechanism, would show today if it had been kept turning.
why: As it stands a stranger can read that the mechanism has in fact been kept turning. The page asks "what the machine would show today if it had been kept turning".
The parenthesis is there to give credit, and the name costs no more words than the description. The notebook's card names him.

old: none sent out before someone else had read it
new: none sent out before a fresh instance of the model had read it
why: "Someone else" can be taken for a person. The box above says the readers were fresh instances of the same model, and Noon's lines say "a fresh instance".
